paragraphs: Writing efficient machine learning libraries requires understanding both the underlying algorithms and the programming languages used for specialized hardware. These architecture-specific languages can be unfamiliar and change quickly, leaving relatively few examples for language models to learn from. The paper examines how an agentic system can help language models tackle this demanding coding setting.

The proposed system improves adaptively through experience it generates itself. It repeatedly uses that experience to strengthen its ability to reason about library development under limited data. The central idea is to make improvement part of the development process, so the system can build on its own accumulated experience when solving complex programming tasks.

The authors construct a benchmark representing a typical machine learning library and evaluate code generation with both open and closed-source language models. They report improvements of up to 3.9 times over a single-model baseline. This supports the usefulness of iterative, self-generated experience for specialized code generation; the reported multiplier concerns benchmark improvement and does not establish a corresponding increase in code execution speed.
icml-2025-adaptive-self-improvement-llm-.tldr: An adaptive agentic system uses self-generated experience to improve specialized ML library code generation, reporting gains of up to 3.9 times over a single-model baseline.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines learning across clients, but the resulting model must often handle data unlike what those clients supplied. One strategy is to extract features causally related to the target label. The paper argues that a shared feature extractor typically retains only causal features common across clients, discarding others that could help under distribution shifts.

FedUni addresses this with two stages. A comprehensive extractor is designed to capture the union of causal feature types present in an input. A following compressor removes potentially inactive causal features. This separates the task of collecting useful information from deciding which information applies to the current input, aiming to preserve more of the benefits of client diversity.

A client-side intervention module further trains the extractor using counterfactual examples that simulate changes in data distribution. Experiments and theoretical analysis support significant improvements in out-of-distribution generalization. The claimed benefit concerns avoiding the feature loss associated with retaining only shared invariances; it should not be read as a claim that federated training eliminates communication or aggregation overhead.
icml-2025-causality-inspired-federated-l.tldr: FedUni combines broad causal feature extraction, selective compression, and counterfactual training to improve federated learning under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Continual test-time adaptation updates a pretrained model as it encounters changing target environments. The paper focuses on environments that return unpredictably and last for different amounts of time. Repeatedly adapting the same parameters can make short visits difficult to learn from, erase earlier knowledge, or carry knowledge into an environment where it does not belong.

DPCore organizes adaptation around visual prompts. Visual Prompt Adaptation aligns the model with the current domain, while a Prompt Coreset preserves previously acquired knowledge. A Dynamic Update mechanism adjusts existing prompts when a new domain resembles earlier ones and creates new prompts when the difference is substantial. Together, these components provide a way to preserve and selectively reuse adaptation.

Across four benchmarks, DPCore outperforms the evaluated continual adaptation methods in both structured and dynamic settings. The authors also report 99% fewer trainable parameters and 64% less computation time than previous approaches. These findings suggest that separating adaptation knowledge across prompts can improve resilience to recurring domain changes while making updates substantially cheaper in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-dpcore-dynamic-prompt-coreset-.tldr: DPCore preserves and selectively updates visual prompts to improve continual adaptation while reducing trainable parameters and computation time.

paragraphs: DDIM inversion depends on accurately approximating the noise involved in reversing a diffusion process. Existing iterative optimization techniques spend computation repeatedly refining that approximation. EasyInv targets this cost by giving greater influence to the initial latent representation, which contains substantial information about the original image.

The method combines the latent state from the preceding time step with the current state in a systematic way. This aggregation strengthens the influence of the initial image information and reduces the impact of noise, avoiding iterative refinement of the noise terms. The approach therefore changes how inversion information is combined rather than relying on repeated correction of each noise estimate.

The authors report inversion results comparable to or better than conventional DDIM inversion, particularly when model precision or computational resources are limited. Relative to off-the-shelf iterative optimization techniques, they report approximately threefold higher inference efficiency. They also state that EasyInv can be combined with most existing inversion methods using four lines of code, suggesting a lightweight route to adopting the aggregation strategy.
icml-2025-easyinv-toward-fast-and-better.tldr: EasyInv aggregates successive latent states to improve diffusion inversion efficiency, reporting roughly threefold gains over iterative optimization techniques.

paragraphs: Decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning lets agents learn collaborative decisions without a central coordinator. Actor-critic methods divide learning between a component that chooses actions and one that evaluates them. Although deep neural versions work well in practice, the paper identifies a theoretical gap: much prior convergence analysis covers linear approximations and guarantees only stationary solutions.

The authors develop a decentralized actor-critic method in which both components are nonlinear neural models. For their proposed method, they establish a global optimality guarantee with a finite-time convergence rate of O(1/T), where T counts iterations. This is stronger than showing that updates eventually reach a stationary point, which alone does not establish global optimality.

The paper presents this as the first global convergence result for deep neural actor-critic methods in the multi-agent reinforcement learning literature. Numerical experiments are reported to verify the theoretical results. The contribution connects a more expressive model class with a quantitative convergence guarantee for the constructed method, rather than establishing the same guarantee for every deep actor-critic algorithm.
icml-2025-finite-time-global-optimality-.tldr: A proposed decentralized deep actor-critic method receives a global optimality guarantee with an O(1/T) finite-time convergence rate.

paragraphs: LoRA reduces fine-tuning memory by learning low-rank changes to model weights. This paper asks whether further savings can come from changing the object being optimized. Its framework focuses on forward states, the intermediate values produced during computation, and treats LoRA as a special case of this broader approach.

State-based tuning introduces parameterized perturbations within the computational graph. These perturbations allow control over states across an entire residual block. A key potential benefit is avoiding storage of large intermediate states in architectures such as transformers. This matters because reducing the number of trainable weights is only one route to lowering the memory needed during adaptation.

Experiments on ViT, RoBERTa, LLaMA2-7B, and LLaMA3-8B report lower memory consumption and computation time alongside improved performance. The authors also explore whether the savings make training 7B and 8B models feasible on consumer GPUs such as the Nvidia 3090 without quantization. That exploration points toward broader hardware accessibility while retaining the abstract's qualified claim about feasibility.
icml-2025-from-weight-based-to-state-bas.tldr: State-based fine-tuning controls intermediate model states to reduce memory and computation beyond LoRA while improving performance in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Ensemble clustering combines multiple clusterings, but its empirical success has outpaced understanding of how well it generalizes. This paper analyzes generalization error, excess risk, and consistency. Its bounds scale as O(sqrt(log(n)/m) + 1/sqrt(n)), where n is the number of samples and m is the number of base clusterings.

The analysis establishes consistency when both quantities grow without bound and m grows sufficiently faster than log(n). For finite ensembles and datasets, the authors instead consider assigning different weights to the available clusterings. Their theory motivates reducing each base clustering's deviation from its expectation while increasing diversity among the clusterings. It also connects diversity maximization approximately to a robust min-max optimization problem.

The authors turn these principles into an ensemble clustering algorithm. Across ten datasets, it reports average improvements of 6.0% in NMI, 7.3% in ARI, and 6.0% in Purity over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution links an asymptotic explanation of generalization to a practical way of choosing how finite clusterings should contribute.
icml-2025-generalization-performance-of-.tldr: Generalization bounds motivate a weighted ensemble clustering algorithm that balances base-clustering bias and diversity.

paragraphs: Kernel methods provide a theoretically established way to learn nonlinear relationships, but their memory demands can make large datasets difficult to handle. The paper identifies another imbalance: much work on scalable kernel learning concentrates on kernel ridge regression. Joker aims to address both the memory burden and the narrower coverage of existing approaches.

Joker supplies a joint optimization framework for kernel ridge regression, logistic regression, and support vector machines. It combines a dual block coordinate descent procedure with a trust-region mechanism and approximates kernels using randomized features. These choices bring optimization and kernel approximation into the same framework, with the stated goal of making several types of kernel model practical at larger scales.

Experiments report memory savings of up to 90% relative to state-of-the-art methods, with comparable or sometimes better training time and predictive performance. The result suggests that substantial memory reduction need not require a corresponding loss of speed or accuracy in the tested settings. Its broader significance is extending that efficiency strategy beyond a single kernel model.
icml-2025-joker-joint-optimization-frame.tldr: Joker combines randomized kernel features with joint optimization to support several kernel models while saving up to 90% memory in experiments.

paragraphs: Splitting large models across GPUs reduces the work and memory assigned to each device, but introduces communication that can limit speed. Ladder Residual addresses this bottleneck through model architecture. It modifies residual connections so communication and computation can overlap, allowing useful computation to proceed while information moves between devices.

The modification is described as applicable to residual-based models, while the paper concentrates on tensor parallelism because of its heavy communication requirements. For a 70-billion-parameter transformer spread across eight devices, applying Ladder Residual throughout the model achieves a reported 29% end-to-end inference speedup. This demonstrates the potential value of designing architecture around distributed execution.

The authors also train 1B and 3B Ladder Transformers from scratch and observe performance comparable to a standard dense transformer. Separately, they show that parts of Llama-3.1 8B can be converted with minimal accuracy degradation after retraining on 3B tokens. These results address both new-model training and partial conversion, with the conversion finding explicitly including additional training.
icml-2025-ladder-residual-parallelism-aw.tldr: Ladder Residual changes model architecture to overlap GPU communication with computation, achieving a reported 29% inference speedup in a 70B-model setting.

paragraphs: This paper asks how single-pass stochastic gradient descent compares with offline kernel regression methods as data increases. The analysis covers an inner-product kernel on the sphere under a source condition, including misspecified cases where the optimal predictor lies outside the kernel's function space. It characterizes excess-risk scaling across sample sizes relative to input dimension.

The central result is that SGD achieves minimax-optimal rates up to constants across these scales, with a specified exception. Unlike ridge regression's saturation behavior, its improvement generally does not hit the same restriction. The authors attribute this advantage to an exponentially decaying step-size schedule, connecting the theoretical result to a schedule also used in deep learning.

The exception concerns highly misspecified models at an extreme late stage, where sample size exceeds every fixed power of input dimension. The result therefore retains a meaningful boundary rather than claiming unrestricted optimality. The analysis additionally establishes what the authors describe as the first provable advantage of this schedule over iterative averaging in the common setting they study.
icml-2025-learning-curves-of-stochastic-.tldr: For the analyzed kernel regression setting, exponentially decaying step sizes let single-pass SGD attain optimal rates across most sample-size regimes without saturation.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated two-player games with finitely many actions. One player, the optimizer, wants to steer a learning opponent toward a Stackelberg equilibrium without knowing that opponent's payoffs. The question is whether observing and interacting with a learner provides enough information to influence its eventual behavior in this way.

The authors first prove an impossibility result: knowing only that the opponent uses some no-regret algorithm is insufficient. That broad behavioral guarantee does not provide enough structure to accomplish the steering objective. This identifies a limit on exploitation based solely on membership in a general class of learning algorithms.

The proposed route forward is to recover the learner's payoff structure from interactions. The authors demonstrate this approach for more restricted algorithm classes, examining an ascent algorithm and stochastic mirror ascent with known regularizer and step sizes. These cases show how additional knowledge about the learner's update mechanism can make steering possible. The positive results depend on that extra structure and do not overturn the impossibility result for arbitrary no-regret learners.
icml-2025-learning-to-steer-learners-in-.tldr: Steering a no-regret learner requires more information than its no-regret guarantee, but recovering payoffs can work for specified learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing aims to change facts stored in a language model. Existing locate-then-edit methods can succeed when a question directly asks for the edited fact, yet struggle when answering requires several linked factual steps. This paper investigates why a successful direct edit may fail to carry through a longer chain of recall.

Using mechanistic interpretability tools, the authors find that multi-hop tasks tend to retrieve knowledge involving implicit subjects from deeper MLP layers. Single-hop recall instead relies on shallower layers. Earlier methods largely target those shallow layers using single-hop prompts, leaving deeper retrieval pathways unchanged. This gives a concrete explanation for the mismatch between direct recall and multi-hop performance.

IFMET responds by locating and editing knowledge in both shallow and deep MLP layers. It uses multi-hop editing prompts alongside single-hop prompts to reach different stages of reasoning. Experiments show significant improvements on multi-hop factual recall. The contribution is therefore both diagnostic and procedural: it identifies a depth-related retrieval difference and uses that finding to broaden where edits are applied.
icml-2025-locate-then-edit-for-multi-hop.tldr: IFMET edits shallow and deep model layers using single-hop and multi-hop prompts to improve recall that depends on newly edited facts.

paragraphs: LoRA adapts language models through low-rank updates, making the directions captured by those updates important. This paper studies how those directions relate to the gradient from one full fine-tuning step. Under gradient descent, the authors prove that LoRA adapters align with particular singular subspaces of that gradient.

The theory suggests initializing adapters from the one-step full gradient so the relevant alignment is present immediately, for both linear and nonlinear models. LoRA-One builds on this initialization principle. The paper also establishes linear convergence and generalization results for its analysis, and shows theoretically how preconditioners can reduce difficulties caused by ill-conditioning.

Experiments report significant gains over LoRA and its variants on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. The analysis additionally connects LoRA-One with other methods based on gradient alignment. The role of the single full-gradient step is to guide the adapter subspace and initialization; the stated result does not mean that all subsequent fine-tuning can universally be replaced by one update.
icml-2025-lora-one-one-step-full-gradien.tldr: LoRA-One uses a single full fine-tuning gradient to initialize aligned adapter subspaces, with theoretical support and empirical gains over LoRA variants.

paragraphs: Simulating interacting physical processes often requires coupling several specialized solvers into one program. Large structures made of many components introduce further computational difficulties. M2PDE approaches both problems by learning how individual processes or components depend on one another, then composing them into a coupled simulation.

During diffusion-based training, the method learns energy functions representing the conditional probability of a process or component given the others. During inference, it samples from a joint probability distribution to generate a coupled solution. The key distinction is between learning conditional relationships locally and using them together when producing the overall physical state.

On reaction-diffusion and nuclear thermal coupling tasks, M2PDE produces more accurate predictions than surrogate models in challenging scenarios. In a prismatic fuel element problem, it scales from training on a single component to a structure with 64 components and outperforms domain-decomposition and graph-based approaches. These results support compositional simulation in the tested settings, especially the possibility of building larger coupled predictions from training at a smaller component scale.
icml-2025-m2pde-compositional-generative.tldr: M2PDE learns conditional physical relationships with diffusion models and composes them into coupled simulations, including a demonstrated 64-component structure.

paragraphs: Building a useful multi-agent language-model system usually requires decisions about how agents act and coordinate. Human-designed frameworks often target a narrow set of scenarios, while automated alternatives can have rigid communication structures or depend on external training data. MetaAgent studies how to generate a coordinated system directly from a task description.

The framework represents the resulting system using a finite state machine. It first designs the multi-agent system and then refines it through an optimization algorithm. At deployment, the state machine governs agent actions and transitions between states. This supplies an explicit structure for controlling execution as the agents work through the task.

The authors evaluate MetaAgent on both text-based and practical tasks. Its generated systems outperform other automatically designed methods and achieve performance comparable to human-designed systems optimized for those tasks. These findings suggest that automated construction can approach specialized manual designs in the evaluated settings. The contribution combines system generation, optimization, and deployment control within a common state-machine framework.
icml-2025-metaagent-automatically-constr.tldr: MetaAgent generates and optimizes multi-agent systems from task descriptions, using finite state machines to control their execution.

paragraphs: Multi-agent systems can extend what a single language-model agent accomplishes, but a fixed workflow may spend similar resources on very different queries. The paper argues that searching for one complex system overlooks variation in task difficulty and domain. It instead makes the architecture used for a query part of the resource-allocation decision.

MaAS optimizes an agentic supernet, described as a continuous probabilistic distribution over agentic architectures. It samples systems from this distribution in a query-dependent way. This lets the framework tailor its use of language-model calls, tool calls, and tokens while pursuing high-quality answers. The search target is thus a distribution of possible workflows rather than a single fixed configuration.

Across six benchmarks, the authors report using only 6–45% of the inference costs of existing handcrafted or automated systems, while surpassing their performance by 0.54–11.82%. They also report stronger transfer across datasets and language-model backbones. Together, these results support adapting collaboration structure to the query as a way to improve both quality and inference efficiency.
icml-2025-multi-agent-architecture-searc.tldr: MaAS samples query-specific multi-agent architectures from an optimized distribution, reporting better performance at 6–45% of comparison systems' inference costs.

paragraphs: Distribution matching usually asks a model to align with a target distribution. This paper considers several targets whose requirements may conflict. Its objective is to characterize Pareto-optimal distributions: tradeoffs for which improving alignment with one target would require sacrificing alignment with another. This turns matching into a problem with several objectives.

The authors develop an information-geometric theory for constructing the Pareto set and its corresponding objective-value front across the exponential family. The analysis covers both KL divergence and its reverse direction. Within that framework, they explicitly derive the set and front for multivariate normal distributions, making the general theory concrete for an important distribution family.

The resulting formulation supports applications such as multiobjective variational autoencoders, which generate image distributions interpolating among multiple targets. Experiments on real-world images show that both proposed algorithms produce high-quality interpolated images. The work connects a mathematical account of competing distribution objectives with generative modeling, providing a structured way to describe and explore compromises among several desired distributions.
icml-2025-multiobjective-distribution-ma.tldr: An information-geometric framework characterizes Pareto-optimal distribution matching and supports generating images that interpolate across multiple target distributions.

paragraphs: BDIA-transformer aims to reduce training memory by making transformer computation exactly reversible at the bit level. It begins by interpreting each transformer block as an Euler approximation to an ordinary differential equation. Bidirectional integration approximation and activation quantization then provide the basis for reversing the computation exactly.

During training, a parameter independently takes the value 0.5 or -0.5 for each sample and block, controlling how consecutive integration approximations are averaged. The authors interpret this as training an ensemble of differential-equation solvers, which regularizes the model. Exact reconstruction also requires storing lightweight side information to recover information lost through quantization.

At inference, the parameter is replaced by its expectation, zero, giving the standard transformer architecture up to activation quantization. Experiments in language generation, image classification, and translation report significantly better validation performance and considerably lower training memory than conventional counterparts. The authors also identify limited-data fine-tuning as a particularly suitable use case because of the ensemble's regularizing effect. Exact reversibility therefore coexists with a small storage requirement and quantized activations.
icml-2025-on-exact-bit-level-reversible-.tldr: BDIA-transformer combines reversible training and randomized integration with lower memory use, retaining standard transformer inference structure up to activation quantization.

paragraphs: Optimization methods differ in how they rescale updates. Layer-wise preconditioning applies transformations along the axes of each layer's weight tensors, whereas methods such as Adam use entry-wise scaling. This paper asks whether the practical appeal of layer-wise methods also reflects a statistical advantage in learning useful representations.

The authors study linear representation learning and single-index learning, two models used to analyze feature learning. They move beyond ideal isotropic Gaussian inputs and well-conditioned settings. In these broader settings, they show theoretically and numerically that SGD can be fundamentally suboptimal at learning features, and that layer-wise preconditioning emerges as a solution to the identified difficulty.

The analysis also finds that Adam-style preconditioning and batch normalization only partly alleviate these problems. The stated necessity of layer-wise preconditioning is grounded in the studied feature-learning problems and their statistical setting. The contribution gives a principled explanation for why accounting for structure across a layer can matter for generalization, beyond the practical observation that an optimizer trains a network effectively.
icml-2025-on-the-concurrence-of-layer-wi.tldr: In two feature-learning models beyond ideal input conditions, layer-wise preconditioning resolves statistical shortcomings that SGD and entry-wise methods do not fully address.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of plausible outcomes to express uncertainty. Streaming data complicates this task because information arrives over time, while privacy requirements constrain how individual observations can influence the output. This paper develops an online framework that addresses uncertainty quantification and individual privacy together.

The method constructs changing, model-free prediction sets using a one-pass algorithm with differential privacy. It therefore does not require repeated access to the full dataset. The authors establish a theoretical guarantee that long-run coverage reaches the nominal confidence level. The long-run qualification matters: the stated guarantee concerns coverage over time rather than a separate certainty claim about every individual prediction.

The framework also extends to conformal quantile regression, adapting to heteroscedasticity, where the amount of uncertainty varies across inputs. Simulations and studies using ELEC2 and PAMAP2 evaluate its effectiveness and applicability. The contribution brings private streaming operation, coverage theory, and adaptation to varying uncertainty into one approach intended for real-time decisions.
icml-2025-online-differentially-private-.tldr: A one-pass private conformal prediction framework produces adaptive prediction sets with theoretical guarantees for long-run coverage.

paragraphs: Theory-of-mind reasoning concerns inferring beliefs, desires, and intentions. Computational systems face growing difficulty when those inferences require multiple planning steps and information from different modalities. This paper proposes a Bayesian planner that divides the reasoning process into successive updates, aiming to make increasing task complexity more manageable.

The approach combines those updates with weak-to-strong control. Smaller language models are specialized to improve the likelihood estimates used in theory-of-mind reasoning. Their reasoning behavior is then transferred to larger language models, spanning 7B to 405B parameters, which contribute social and world knowledge. The method connects specialized estimation with the broader knowledge available in larger models.

Experiments on multimodal theory-of-mind benchmarks, including unseen scenarios, report a 4.6% accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support this combination of stepwise probabilistic reasoning and model specialization in the evaluated tasks. The contribution is a way to organize inference about mental states as task demands grow, with the reported evidence coming from benchmark accuracy rather than a claim of human-equivalent social understanding.
icml-2025-overcoming-multi-step-complexi.tldr: A Bayesian planner combines stepwise belief updates with small-to-large model transfer, reporting a 4.6% accuracy improvement on multimodal theory-of-mind benchmarks.

paragraphs: Generating synthetic images from a small private dataset is especially relevant in specialized domains where examples are scarce. Existing Private Evolution uses diffusion-model APIs and private similarity voting, but the paper identifies weaknesses when only a few private examples are available. PCEvolve seeks to extract more useful guidance from that limited data.

Its iterative process mines contrastive relationships between classes rather than relying only on information about individual examples. It incorporates those relationships into an adapted Exponential Mechanism within the evolution loop. This combines a richer signal for evaluating generated data with the differential-privacy mechanism used to guide the process.

Experiments on four specialized datasets show that PCEvolve outperforms Private Evolution and other API-assisted baselines. The results support the value of inter-class relationships for improving synthetic image generation in the few-shot private setting. More broadly, the approach uses generative API access together with private-data-based quality evaluation, offering a route to useful synthetic datasets without abandoning the stated differential-privacy objective.
icml-2025-pcevolve-private-contrastive-e.tldr: PCEvolve uses private inter-class contrastive relationships to improve API-assisted synthetic image generation from few-shot private data.

paragraphs: Preference training often records which response is better while overlooking how good either response actually is. The paper argues that this can penalize a strong response merely because another is slightly better, or encourage a weak response because its alternative is worse. Both problems arise from treating relative preference as the whole training signal.

The proposed approach uses reward scores already available from judge models. It relabels preference pairs to condition them on quality scores, producing a reward-augmented dataset and reward-conditioned language-model policies. This allows training to distinguish different levels of response quality and aims to help the model generalize toward better responses that are sparse in the original data.

Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks consistently improve DPO by a considerable margin. Ablation studies also support reduced unlearning of useful responses and show benefits beyond simply expanding the dataset. The central finding is that preserving quality information within preference training can make better use of the same underlying judgments and reduce harmful pressure against relatively rejected but valuable answers.
icml-2025-reward-augmented-data-enhances.tldr: Conditioning preference data on reward scores improves DPO and helps reduce unlearning of high-quality rejected responses.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks commonly learn by passing information between connected neighbors. Hierarchical pooling adds clustering so the model can build larger-scale representations. The paper argues that strong dependence on graph connectivity limits how well these methods capture the richer geometry available in geometric graphs.

The proposed Rhomboid Tiling clustering method uses a geometric tiling structure to form clusters. Its purpose is to exploit complex geometric information and extract higher-order geometric structures, bringing information beyond neighborhood connectivity into the clustering process. The authors then build RTPool, a hierarchical pooling model that uses these clusters for graph classification.

RTPool outperforms 21 state-of-the-art competitors on all seven benchmark datasets reported in the abstract. This provides empirical support for using geometric structure to guide hierarchical graph representations. The contribution lies both in the geometry-based clustering method and in showing how it can serve a graph classification model. The reported breadth concerns the evaluated competitors and datasets, rather than a universal ranking of graph-learning methods.
icml-2025-rhomboid-tiling-for-geometric-.tldr: RTPool uses rhomboid-tiling-based geometric clustering and outperforms 21 comparison methods across seven graph classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Koopman theory represents nonlinear dynamics through a linear operator acting on measurement functions of the system. Its practical difficulty is that this operator is generally infinite-dimensional. A forecasting model therefore needs measurement functions that support a manageable finite-dimensional approximation while retaining useful information about the dynamics.

The paper connects that approximation problem to linear recurrent neural networks. By extending the state to include lagged observations, the authors establish an equivalence between a structured Koopman operator and linear recurrent updates. This gives a theoretical basis for implementing the operator through a sequence-model architecture with highly parallel computation.

SKOLR combines a learnable spectral decomposition of the input signal with a multilayer perceptron to define its measurement functions. A stack of linear recurrent networks implements the structured operator. Experiments on forecasting benchmarks and dynamical systems report strong performance. The contribution joins the representation-learning role of nonlinear measurement functions with linear recurrent evolution, translating a dynamical-systems framework into a streamlined forecasting design.
icml-2025-skolr-structured-koopman-opera.tldr: SKOLR connects structured Koopman operators with linear recurrent networks to build a parallelizable time-series forecasting model.
